title: How do you add the brand's required wording to a script naturally?
description: How to place a brand's required lines in a UGC script so they sound like you: keep the wording exact, change what surrounds it, and deliver it naturally.
short_answer: Keep the brand's required wording exactly as written and change everything around it instead. Give each fixed line a moment in the script where it answers something the viewer has just seen, lead into it with a short line in your own voice, and deliver it at your normal pace rather than reading it out.

sections.heading: Can you change the brand's required wording to make it sound better?

blocks.text: Do not change a required line, even slightly, unless the brand agrees to a new version in writing first.

A line the [brief](/glossary/#brief) marks as fixed is there for a reason you may not see: approval from another team, a promise the brand has made elsewhere, or a phrase it uses everywhere. Swapping one word can send the video back for a reshoot. So treat the wording as locked and treat its surroundings as yours. If a line truly will not sit in your mouth, ask the brand before you film whether a softer version is allowed, and keep the reply with your notes.

This is a different job from squeezing several selling points into a short video. [Fitting the brand's key points into a short UGC script](/blog/fit-key-points-into-ugc-script/) covers ideas you may phrase your own way. Required wording is the narrower case: the words themselves are fixed.

sections.heading: Where in the script should a required line go?

blocks.text: Put each required line straight after the moment that makes it relevant, so it lands as an answer rather than an announcement.

Read each fixed line and ask what the viewer would need to have just seen for it to make sense. A line about how a product feels belongs after the close-up. A line about what is in the box belongs after you open it. Then place it in that [beat](/glossary/#beat), not in the opening line, unless the brief says otherwise, because the opening has to stay about the viewer. The section on [where the brand's required lines go](/blog/brief-to-script/#placing-required-lines) shows how to mark them up before you start drafting.

table_rows: A product name or full product title
The first beat after the problem
The viewer now wants to know what you reached for.
A feature phrase written by the brand
Right after the shot that shows that feature
The picture proves it while you say it.
Near the end, before the ask
It reads as a summary instead of a pitch.
A line the brief asks you to say about the post itself
Where the brief places it, said plainly
The brand decides this one, so follow it exactly.

sections.heading: How do you lead into a fixed line so it sounds like you?

blocks.text: Write a short bridge in your own words just before the fixed line, so your voice carries the viewer into it.

A required line sounds scripted when it arrives cold, straight after a different thought. A bridge gives it a reason to be said. Keep bridges short and plain, and make them about what you noticed, not about the product's claims.

items: Point at the screen: here is the bit I actually checked, then the fixed line.
Admit you are quoting: the box puts it like this, then the fixed line. This works when the wording is formal, because you are not pretending it is how you talk.
Ask the viewer's question for them: so what is it actually made of, then the fixed line.
Follow it with a short line of your own, such as that was the part I cared about, so you end the beat in your own voice.
Cut any bridge that repeats the fixed line in other words, since saying it twice makes both versions sound rehearsed.

blocks.text: If you want more on keeping the rest of the script in your own voice, read [how to write a UGC script in your own voice](/blog/ugc-script-in-your-own-voice/).

sections.heading: What does a script look like with a required line built in?

blocks.text: Here the brand's fixed line is built from placeholders, and every line around it is written to lead into it.

blocks.script_caption: Example script — written for this answer, for a refillable glass water bottle with a tea infuser

script_beats.say: I keep leaving tea bags to stew in a mug on my desk until they taste like the bottom of a pond.
script_beats.do: Close shot of a dark, cold mug of tea next to a laptop, a soggy tea bag hanging over the rim.

script_beats.say: So this week I have been carrying my tea around instead.
script_beats.do: Pick up the glass bottle from the desk and turn it so the infuser basket inside is visible.

script_beats.say: The leaves go in here. The box puts it like this: [PRODUCT] keeps your leaves in and your tea clear.
script_beats.do: Unscrew the top, spoon loose leaves into the basket, and hold it up to the light.

script_beats.say: That was the part I cared about, because I hate bits in my teeth.
script_beats.do: Pour a glass from the bottle and hold it to the window so the clear tea shows.

script_beats.say: And when it is strong enough, the basket just lifts out.
script_beats.do: Lift the infuser out, tap it on the sink edge, and screw the lid back on.

script_beats.say: I will link the one I use, if your desk has a pond mug too.
script_beats.do: Set the bottle down next to the old mug, then nudge the mug out of frame.

blocks.text: Notice that the required line sits after the shot of the basket, is flagged as the brand's wording, and is followed by a line of your own. Nothing in the fixed line has been altered.

sections.heading: How do you deliver a fixed line on camera without reading it?

blocks.text: Learn the fixed line until you can say it while doing the action, and film that beat as its own short take.

items: Say the line out loud while doing the action several times before you record, because your hands give your voice a rhythm to follow.
Film the beat with the fixed line separately, so a stumble costs you one short take, not the whole video.
Keep your pace the same as the lines around it. Slowing down for the fixed line is what makes it sound like an advert.
Check the take against the brief word by word before you move on, since a small slip is easy to miss on playback.

sections.heading: What should you send the brand with the script?

blocks.text: Send the script with every required line highlighted, so the brand can confirm the wording before you film.

A highlighted line lets the person approving the [script](/glossary/#script) check it in seconds and see that the rest is yours. Add a short note such as: Required lines are highlighted and copied exactly from the brief dated [DATE]. Let me know if any wording has changed. That catches an updated brief before it turns into a reshoot.

hooks: I keep leaving tea bags to stew in a mug on my desk until they taste like the bottom of a pond.
